section_title: How does David make Solomon’s kingship public?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 28 Then King David said, “Call in Bathsheba for me.” So she came into the king’s presence and stood before him. 29 And the king swore an oath, saying, “As surely as the LORD lives, who has redeemed my life from all distress, 30 I will carry out this very day exactly what I swore to you by the LORD, the God of Israel: Surely your son Solomon will reign after me, and he will sit on my throne in my place.” 31 Bathsheba bowed facedown in homage to the king and said, “May my lord King David live forever!”

32 Then King David said, “Call in for me Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada.” So they came before the king. 33 “Take my servants with you,” said the king. “Set my son Solomon on my own mule and take him down to Gihon. 34 There Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet are to anoint him king over Israel. You are to blow the ram’s horn and declare, ‘Long live King Solomon!’ 35 Then you shall go up with him, and he is to come and sit on my throne and reign in my place. For I have appointed him ruler over Israel and Judah.” 36 “Amen,” replied Benaiah son of Jehoiada. “May the LORD, the God of my lord the king, so declare it. 37 Just as the LORD was with my lord the king, so may He be with Solomon and make his throne even greater than that of my lord King David.”

38 Then Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada, along with the Cherethites and Pelethites, went down and set Solomon on King David’s mule, and they escorted him to Gihon. 39 Zadok the priest took the horn of oil from the tabernacle and anointed Solomon. Then they blew the ram’s horn, and all the people proclaimed, “Long live King Solomon!” 40 All the people followed him, playing flutes and rejoicing with such a great joy that the earth was split by the sound.

context_lines: David recalls the LORD who has redeemed his life from distress and renews his oath to Bathsheba. Solomon will sit on his throne, and David will act that very day.

He orders Zadok, Nathan and Benaiah to take Solomon to Gihon on his own mule. Solomon is to be anointed, proclaimed king and brought back to sit on David’s throne. Benaiah prays that God will be with Solomon and make his throne greater than David’s.

The instructions are carried out. Zadok anoints Solomon, the ram’s horn sounds and the people rejoice loudly. Unlike Adonijah’s self-promotion, this public action carries the reigning king’s express authorization.
common_interpretation_lines: [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-kings/) and [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/1.htm) understand the use of David’s own mule as a sign of his consent to Solomon’s succession. The significance lies especially in whose animal it is.

Wesley reads Solomon’s taking the throne while David is alive as delegated rule that becomes sole kingship after David’s death. [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_kings/1.htm) stresses the people’s joy at Solomon’s elevation.
The scene brings together David’s decision, the priest’s anointing, the prophet’s participation and the people’s welcome. It answers the question that has driven the chapter.
god_plan_lines: This royal entry offers a useful comparison with Jesus entering Jerusalem in [Matthew 21:1–11](https://biblehub.com/bsb/matthew/21.htm). The people there acclaim Him as the Son of David, and Matthew identifies His coming with the promised gentle King.

The animals are different: Solomon rides David’s mule, while Matthew describes a donkey and her colt. Matthew explicitly connects Jesus’ entry with the prophetic promise he quotes; he does not say that Solomon’s procession is that prophecy.

The parallel concerns the public welcome of a Davidic king. Alongside it stands [Luke 1:32–33](https://biblehub.com/bsb/luke/1.htm), which promises Jesus David’s throne and a kingdom without end. Solomon’s succession continues the family line; Jesus is the King whose reign endures.
